claims.claim: US guidance for older people in long-term care defines fever as a single oral temperature above 37.8 C, repeated oral readings above 37.2 C (or rectal above 37.5 C), or a single temperature more than 1.1 C above the person's baseline from any site.
claims.supporting_passage: Stone 2012: "The definition of fever was changed from a temperature of greater than 38°C (100.4°F), as in the original McGeer Criteria, to a definition consistent with the 2008 Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) guideline for evaluating fever and infection in older adults residing in LTCFs: either (1) a single oral temperature greater than 37.8°C (100°F) or (2) repeated oral temperatures greater than 37.2°C (99°F) or rectal temperatures greater than 37.5°C (99.5°F) or (3) a single temperature greater than 1.1°C (2°F) over baseline from any site." Table 2: "A. Fever 1. Single oral temperature >37.8°C (>100°F) OR 2. Repeated oral temperatures >37.2°C (99°F) or rectal temperatures >37.5°C (99.5°F) OR 3. Single temperature >1.1°C (2°F) over baseline from any site (oral, tympanic, axillary)"
claims.location: Stone 2012, Definitions: Constitutional Criteria for Infection (p. 5) and Table 2 (p. 14)
claims.pico_timeframe: Residents of long-term care facilities; expert definitions consistent with the IDSA 2008 guideline; no outcome or timeframe
claims.safe_wording: US infection guidance for older people living in care homes counts as a fever: one oral reading above 37.8°C, repeated oral readings above 37.2°C, or any reading more than 1.1°C above the person's usual temperature. The rise-from-usual rule applies to ear, mouth or armpit readings.
claims.qualifications: Say it comes from US guidance for care home residents (IDSA 2008, as restated in the 2012 revised McGeer surveillance criteria). The IDSA guideline full text itself was not opened. Do not present as UK guidance.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Written for care home residents, where usual readings may be recorded; in an emergency department the usual temperature is often not known. No sensitivity or specificity for these thresholds was opened.

numbers.meaning: single oral reading threshold for fever
repeated oral readings threshold
repeated rectal readings threshold
rise over the person's baseline from any site (oral, tympanic, axillary)

claims.claim: Typical fever is often absent in older people with serious infection.
claims.supporting_passage: High 2009 abstract: "Most residents are older and have multiple comorbidities that complicate recognition of infection; for example, typically defined fever is absent in more than one-half of LTCF residents with serious infection." Norman 2000 abstract: "Fever, the cardinal sign of infection, may be absent or blunted 20%-30% of the time." Stone 2012: "The lower threshold will increase sensitivity for detecting infection given the greater likelihood of a lower febrile response in the elderly."
claims.location: High 2009 Abstract; Norman 2000 Abstract; Stone 2012 Definitions: Constitutional Criteria (p. 5)
claims.pico_timeframe: Care home residents with serious infection (High); older adults in general (Norman review)
claims.safe_wording: Many older people with a serious infection do not develop a typical fever. US care home guidance says typical fever is absent in more than half of residents with serious infection; an earlier review put fever absent or blunted in 20 to 30 in 100 older people with infection.
claims.qualifications: Either say 'often' without a number, or give both figures with their populations. Do not say 'more than half of older people' without 'living in care homes'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The two estimates differ (more than 1 in 2 versus 1 in 5 to 3 in 10) and neither primary study was opened. The claim that older people have lower baseline temperatures was NOT found in the sources opened; Stone supports only a 'lower febrile response'. Do not say older people run colder.

numbers.meaning: care home residents with serious infection without typically defined fever (IDSA abstract)
older people with infection in whom fever is absent or blunted (Norman review)

claims.claim: NEWS2 gives 0 points for temperatures from 36.1 to 38.0 C.
claims.supporting_passage: Engebretsen 2020, Table 1 'NEWS2 and OUH-criteria', Temperature (°C) row: 3 points "≤35.0"; 1 point "35.1–36.0"; 0 points "36.1–38.0"; 1 point "38.1–39.0"; 2 points "≥39.1". NEWS2 is cited to: "Royal College of Physicians. National Early Warning Score (NEWS) 2: Standardising the Assessment of Acute-Illness Severity in the NHS. London: RCP; 2017."
claims.pico_timeframe: NEWS2 scoring chart (RCP 2017) as reproduced in a peer-reviewed paper
claims.safe_wording: On NEWS2, any temperature from 36.1°C to 38.0°C scores 0. A temperature has to reach 38.1°C to score 1 point.
claims.qualifications: Cite the Royal College of Physicians NEWS2 chart (2017) via this reproduction; the RCP document could not be opened here.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None on the bands. Temperature is one of six parameters; the total score, not temperature alone, drives escalation.

band scoring 1

band scoring 1

claims.claim: NEWS2 has no adjustment for age, and a low score should never override a clinician's or carer's concern.
claims.supporting_passage: Vardy 2022: "The National Early Warning Score (NEWS), published in 2012, made no specific adjustments for older people." "Insufficient evidence was available to apply weighting to the NEWS score to account for age." "Study of performance of the NEWS2 specifically in older people is important, as the physiological and vital sign changes seen in response to acute illness may differ for older adults, as well as their acute care preferences." Williams 2022: "An important point emphasised in the original NEWS report, and reiterated subsequently, is that a low score should never override a healthcare professional or carer's concern about a patient's clinical condition if they feel it is necessary to escalate care."
claims.location: Vardy 2022 Abstract and 'NEWS2 in older people in hospital' (pp. 522-3); Williams 2022 p. 3
claims.pico_timeframe: NEWS/NEWS2 in the NHS; older people
claims.safe_wording: NEWS2 has no adjustment for age. Its developers say a low score should never override a professional's or carer's concern about a patient.
claims.qualifications: Vardy is expert commentary; the Williams statement reports the RCP position.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Neither source addresses temperature thresholds in older people specifically.

claims.claim: Illustrative example: for a person whose usual temperature is 36.0 C, a reading of 37.5 C scores 0 on NEWS2 but is a rise of 1.5 C, which meets the care home guidance definition of fever (more than 1.1 C over baseline).
claims.supporting_passage: Engebretsen 2020 Table 1: 0 points "36.1–38.0". Stone 2012 Table 2: "3. Single temperature >1.1°C (2°F) over baseline from any site (oral, tympanic, axillary)"
claims.pico_timeframe: Illustrative arithmetic combining two definitions
claims.safe_wording: Illustrative example: if someone's usual temperature is 36.0°C, a reading of 37.5°C scores nothing on NEWS2, yet it is 1.5°C above their usual, which US care home guidance would count as a fever.
claims.qualifications: Must be labelled 'Illustrative example'. Do not state that older people typically run at 36.0°C (not supported).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Whether the IDSA baseline rule improves detection in emergency departments was not examined in any source opened.

candidates.reason: All essential claims supported: care home fever definitions including the >1.1°C rise over baseline (Stone 2012 full text restating IDSA 2008; High 2009 abstract), NEWS2 scores 0 for 36.1 to 38.0°C (Engebretsen 2020 Table 1 reproducing RCP 2017), NEWS2 has no age adjustment and a low score should not override concern (Vardy 2022; Williams 2022). Wording limits: the IDSA fever definitions are for care home residents; 'more than half' applies only to care home residents with serious infection and conflicts with a 20 to 30% review estimate (Norman 2000); the claim that older people have lower baseline temperatures was not found and must go; the 36.0/37.5 example must be labelled illustrative; the advice on where to find a baseline is a suggestion, not a finding.

Vaughn 2019 (full text) supports 67.8% excess, 93.2% of excess from discharge prescriptions, only 32.1% with duration documented and documentation linked with fewer excess days (aRR 0.78), and 5% higher odds of patient-reported side effects per excess day with no benefit. Population is US adults of all ages (median age 70). Drop the C. difficile age claim: this study found no link between extra days and C. difficile (0.5% vs 0.5%). NICE 5-day wording is a search extract only; use the PTC trial (Dinh 2021) if a short-course statement is wanted.

Kehoe 2015 (1990 to 2013 shift to low falls; over-75s 26.9%), Bulger 2000 (mortality 22% vs 10%; OR 1.19 per rib; quote no pneumonia per-rib figure), prehospital under-triage of older people (Alshibani 2021; Lupton 2022) and about 5% intracranial bleeding after a fall (de Wit 2020) are supported. The anticoagulant element of the position is contradicted by a 2025 meta-analysis (anticoagulant not a risk factor for intracranial bleeding after ground-level-fall head injury, OR 0.8) and must go; the TARN 2017 trauma-team/senior-review claim and NICE NG39 were not opened and must go.
candidates.revised_angle: Registry data show that by 2013 the commonest cause of major trauma in England and Wales was a fall from less than 2 metres, with about 1 in 4 cases over 75; triage rules built on mechanism miss serious injury in older people more often. Close on one instruction without anticoagulants: after a low fall in an older person, look for head and chest injury (about 1 in 20 who attend after a fall have bleeding inside the skull; older people with rib fractures die about twice as often as younger adults with similar injuries) rather than judging by the height of the fall.

candidates.reason: Jones 2022 abstract supports the dataset, the linear rise from 5 to 12 hours, the 8% SMR step at 6 to 8 hours, the 1-in-82 estimate and the adjustment list. Wording must change: the model did not adjust for acute illness severity ('adjusted for illness' is wrong); the comparison group behind 1 in 82 could not be verified (full text inaccessible), so it must be presented as the authors' estimate from observed versus expected deaths, not 'compared with shorter waits'; the authors' causal wording must not be repeated. Older-people evidence added: older adults more often stay 4 hours or more (Ogliari 2022, single English site) and overnight ED stays for people 75+ were linked with higher mortality in France (Roussel 2023) but not clearly in Spain (Miro 2024).
candidates.revised_angle: Read the most-quoted English study properly: over 5 million admissions, mortality rose with each hour beyond 5 hours up to 12, and the authors estimated 1 extra death per 82 people delayed beyond 6 to 8 hours. It allowed for age, long-term conditions, deprivation and crowding but not for how ill people were on arrival, and it shows a link, not proof. Add the older-person picture: older people wait longer (79 in 100 visits by people 85+ lasted 4 hours or more in one English department), and overnight waits for people 75+ were linked with more deaths in France but not clearly in Spain.

candidates.reason: Essential claims supported with qualifications: new pressure sores during an ED stay (Dugaret 2014 full text: 4.9% overall, 15.7% in over-75s, mostly stage I on heels and sacrum, mean stay 9.1 hours); older people wait longer (Ogliari 2022); time-critical medicines such as Parkinson's are often late or missed and missed doses are linked with harm (Richard 2022; Lertxundi 2017, inpatient studies). The candidate's claim that longer stays are independently associated with sores is not supported after adjustment and must not be made. Drinking and toilet requests carry no evidence claim and stay as questions. NPSA RRR009 was not opened; do not cite. Schedule apart from C15-14 as the editor directed.
